name: HD 95086 dust ring
description: The broad belt of dust around Aiolos (HD 95086), brightest about 200 au from the star, in its own glow at 1.3 millimetres, as ALMA imaged it in April and May 2015 (project 2013.1.00612.S), in the color scale Su et al. (2017) show it in. The giant planet b orbits inside it. One unit is one astronomical unit; the ring's size and tilt are the ones Su et al. fitted, its depth is that tilted ring, and its thickness and which side is nearer are conventions, not measurements.

datasets.label: ALMA · dust ring, 1.3 mm
datasets.title: The dust ring around Aiolos (HD 95086) in its own glow at 1.3 millimetres, from ALMA
datasets.summary: The broad belt of dust around the star, brightest about 200 au out, in its own glow at 1.3 mm, as ALMA imaged it. Planet b orbits inside it.
datasets.description: ALMA observed the star six times between 10 April and 2 May 2015 at 1.3 millimetres (project 2013.1.00612.S). What it sees is the dust's own faint heat, not starlight. This is the image the ARI-L project made from those observations for the public archive, brought to the resolution of the map Su et al. (2017) made from them together with a second set of observations, and shown in the color scale of their map of the disc alone (Figure 3, right). It holds half the data of theirs and is noisier: 12.8 µJy per beam against their 7.5. Two sources behind the ring are removed as the points Su et al. subtract; they find the bright one consistent with a distant galaxy. What is left of it, the brightest spot on the ring's west side, is in their map too and is not known to be dust. The ring's size and tilt are Su et al.'s fit: brightest 200 au from the star at the distance they adopt (206 au at Gaia's distance), 168 au wide and tilted 30°. The image has no third axis, so the depth is inferred: each line of sight is placed on that tilted ring, which projects to the image better than a spherical shell or a constant depth. Its thickness and which side is nearer are conventions; no observation gives them. Su et al. do not detect the star at this wavelength. The star itself is the sphere at the centre, and planet b orbits inside the ring.

archive.limitation: The image is the ARI-L project’s, not the paper’s own: made from one of the two data sets the paper combines (its data set B), with other weighting and cleaning, and meant to show what the data hold, not as a final science image. At the paper’s resolution its noise is 12.8 µJy per beam against the paper’s 7.5 for both sets. It holds the paper’s flux: 2.73 mJy inside 4.8″ in the ring’s plane with the two points removed, against 2.79 ± 0.1. What is left of the bright background source after its point is removed, up to 189 µJy per beam on the ring’s west side, is in the paper’s own map of the disc too and is drawn; it is not known to be dust. Emission fainter than the drawn noise is not claimed.

pointSources.source: Su et al. (2017), AJ 154, 225, arXiv:1709.10129, Table 3: the two point sources they subtract to make their map of the disc alone (Figure 3, right), from a fit to the long baselines of both data sets: 0.81 ± 0.03 mJy at 3.08″ west and 0.83″ north of the star, and 0.10 ± 0.02 mJy at 2.80″ west and 1.61″ south. They take the star at the pointing centre, which is this image's reference position, and the offsets are counted from it. They find the bright one consistent with a star-forming galaxy far behind the star. A point source's peak per beam is its flux, whatever the beam

smoothTo.source: the beam of the map Su et al. (2017, section 3.1) made from both data sets, 1.22″ × 1.03″ at 77.4°, with natural weighting; their map of the disc alone (Figure 3, right) is of that data. This image's ARI-L weighting gave 1.152″ × 0.991″ at 75.5°

colorMap.source: the color bar of Su et al. (2017), Figure 3, right panel, decoded from the figure in the paper's arXiv source: linear in signal-to-noise ratio, labelled from −7 to 35. The paper gives the noise of the map made from both data sets as 7.5 µJy per beam (section 3.1); times that, the listed colors run from −52.33 to 261.98 µJy per beam. Reading the bar's unit as that noise is this recipe's, not a statement of the paper's caption

noiseFade.source: Stated, a display choice: a column fades in as its brightness rises from two to three times its per-pixel noise (12.8 µJy per beam, measured 5.5 to 8.5 arcseconds out), so empty sky is not drawn; three times the noise is the lowest contour Su et al. (2017) draw. The low end of this color scale is a saturated blue, not a dark color, so sky left in would be drawn as bright as the ring. Every channel of a column is scaled alike, so no color changes.

datasets.stellarFluxSource: Not divided by the star: at 1.3 mm the ring is the dust's own thermal emission, not scattered starlight, and it is shown in its own brightness, Jy per beam.
datasets.innerMaskSource: No mask: an interferometer image has no coronagraph, and Su et al. (2017, section 3.4) do not detect the star at 1.3 mm, so nothing is removed at the centre. The star is the host body's own sphere.
datasets.nearSideSource: the north end of the minor axis is drawn nearer, a convention; this image does not say which end is. The minor axis is the ring's position angle, 97°, less 90°
datasets.heightSource: a convention, the height the PDS 70 and HD 181327 rings are drawn with. Su et al. (2017, section 3.1) model the ring as geometrically thin, with no scale height, and at 30° from face-on the image cannot resolve a thickness
datasets.adoptPublishedRing: what is left of the bright source after its point is removed lies on the ring's west side and pulls the ridge traced on this image (189 au, 38°, position angle 93°); Su et al. (2017) fit a gaussian ring to these observations and their data set A together, with that source masked or modelled (section 3.4, Table 4). They print 200 ± 6 au and 168 ± 7 au at the 83.8 pc they adopt, 2.39″ and 2.00″ on the sky, which are 206.4 and 173.3 au at Gaia DR3's 86.46 pc
